cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and what you opened as a question now has its edges.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: Pick one way to go, from what you actually want rather than what the arithmetic says, and stay pointed that way for three days. No re-surveying. Then see what held.
cells.core:
Something you opened without knowing the outcome has a shape you can stand on. You know its edges and what it took, and you're not trying to turn it into something else. That isn't coasting — that's having arrived somewhere real, and the weight is real weight.

The next move is smaller than it feels. What this wants now is a heading, and the heading is yours to set. Set it from appetite, not arithmetic, and hold it for three days without checking the alternatives again. The hard part is behind you. The finished thing is the ground your next direction gets set from — not a ruling on which direction is permitted.

cells.tense: You are bracing for the next demand the finished work will make before you have actually met it.
cells.act: see the thing as if for the first time
cells.ask: Once this week, take something plainly there and give it five plain lines — color, placement, movement. No conclusions. Then set the pen down.
cells.core:
The work is finished, and you're already three steps past it — planning the launch, rehearsing the critique, deciding what it all means before you've set it down. The future you're composing can't be composed yet. It's going to differ from the draft. You're carrying the weight of something done by refusing to put it down.

That refusal thinks it's preventing something. It isn't. Take something plainly there and give it five plain lines — color, placement, movement. No conclusions. What you take in comes first and the meaning comes after, and you don't have to force either one. Let the thing show itself before you decide what it's for.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that is already behind you, still waiting for permission to be done.
cells.act: leave the heart open and empty a while
cells.ask: Somewhere unfamiliar, with your palms open and nothing planned, let whatever comes come. Don't sort it or name it afterward.
cells.core:
Something you made is finished, and you're still stationed near where it happened, holding the old handle, waiting on a signal that it counted. You gave the work what it needed. You don't owe it more of yourself to prove it occurred. A finished thing is finished by fact, not by verdict.

What brings you back isn't more effort on it. It's your own open hands. Somewhere unfamiliar, with your palms empty — nothing to write, nothing to scroll — let whatever comes, come. You're not hunting a feeling and you're not deciding what the experience means. You're letting the next moment reach you unprepared. It may be dull. That's fine. The threshold doesn't need you standing on it.

cells.tense: You are steering the finished thing without counting yourself as the one steering it.
cells.act: join someone in the work so the two streams run as one
cells.ask: Bring what you made to one person who cares about it, describe the real draft rather than the polished report, and take the next step together.
cells.core:
You made the thing — you did make it — but when you talk about it you stand off to the side, as if it assembled itself and you happened to be nearby. The choices were yours. The deciding was yours. You're carrying the finished product with your name left off it.

What brings you back is putting it between you and one other person. Bring what you made to someone who cares about it, describe the real draft instead of the polished report, and take the next move together — two people through one problem rather than you alone at the workbench. That isn't a pitch and it isn't a plan. It's letting someone else see the thing as yours, and letting the honest version of it do some work in the open.
cells.sheetLine: You made it. Set it between you and someone who cares.
